results:
The search returned one article, Proton's blog post on Google's selfie video verification, repeated across about ten language versions. I found no Google documentation, so these are a third-party account.

- **Storage:** The article says enrollment records a video that Google keeps on its own servers as the reference, rather than on the device.
- **Phone option:** It says the feature offers no way to keep the reference on your phone, even though face unlock uses a separate per-device reference.
- **Matching and access:** Matching runs server-side, which the article says lets Google decrypt the video.
- **Deletion:** Per Google's general privacy policy as quoted by Proton, deleted data can persist for about 2 months in active systems and up to 6 months in backups, longer for security, fraud, or legal reasons.
- **AI training:** Google reportedly says the video is used only for sign-in and that helping improve its verification technology is optional. Proton notes it is unclear whether that covers only face matching or broader AI training.
- **Anti-spoofing:** Liveness checks, synthetic-media detection, and, on some devices, hardware signals are meant to block photos and deepfakes.

For primary confirmation, check Google's account help pages and privacy policy directly.

content.title: Introducing selfie for sign-in: a new, easy way to access your Google Account
Google Selfie Video Sign-in: How It Works and Who Can Use It
Google has a new way to sign in to your account—and it uses your face
You Can Now Use A Selfie Video To Sign In To Your Google Account — Here's How
Google introduces new 'selfie video' sign-in method
Google's newest sign-in method asks you to look at the camera - Help Net Security
Selfie sign-in FAQ - Google Account Community
Google Selfie Video Sign-In: Should You Use It?
Google Selfie Video Sign-In: What It Is and How to Set It Up

results:
I couldn't find a Google blog post dated October 15, 2026. The main Google announcement appears to be from late July 2026, and the results describe the feature as rolling out since then.

**What it is:** A backup way to regain access to a Google Account when you're locked out. Google's own post says the video is recorded with guided head movements to verify your identity, and it remains encrypted and under your control. It is optional and is not a replacement for passwords or passkeys.

**Enrollment:** You look at your device's camera and make head movements so Google captures your face from several angles. One outlet says the recording gets encrypted and saved to your Google Account.

**Sign-in:** You record a fresh selfie, and Google matches it against the saved reference. Liveness checks ask for movements to confirm a live person is present. Google also runs its standard checks for suspicious sign-ins.

**Storage and deletion:** Google says it is recorded and securely stored with your consent, and you can delete it at any time in your Google Account. One source adds that Google says it may retain selfie videos for longer if a user violates its policies. Another says an optional opt-in lets data be used to improve verification methods.

**Eligibility:** Workspace accounts, children, and people enrolled in the Advanced Protection Program don't qualify. It is not available for all regions, accounts, or devices.
